title: Chapter 11 — Laundry
intro: Front load vs. top load, capacity truths, pedestals and stacking, and dryer technology.

sections.title: The Great Debate: Front-Load vs Top-Load
content: This is the first question in every laundry sale. The customer either has an opinion or they need you to guide them. Know both sides cold.

**Top-Load with Agitator.** The traditional washing machine. A central post agitates clothes through the water. Advantages: familiar, fast cycles, easy to add forgotten items mid-cycle, less bending to load. Disadvantages: uses more water, harder on fabrics, smaller usable capacity because the agitator takes up space. This is still the #1 selling configuration in North America. Brands: Maytag, Whirlpool, Amana, GE, Samsung, LG. Don't dismiss top-load customers — they know what they like.

**Top-Load with Impeller.** No agitator post — a low-profile disc at the bottom creates currents that move clothes through the water. HE (high efficiency) — uses less water. Larger usable capacity than agitator models in the same drum size. Gentler on clothes. Some customers feel clothes don't get as clean because they can't see aggressive agitation. Samsung and LG have pushed impeller top-loads heavily.

**Front-Load.** Door on the front, horizontal drum tumbles clothes through a shallow pool of water. HE standard. Best cleaning performance in independent tests. Largest capacities (5.0+ cu ft). Best spin speeds (removes more water, reducing dryer time). Uses the least water and energy. Stackable — critical for space-constrained installations. Disadvantages: must bend to load/unload, door seal requires maintenance (wipe it dry to prevent mold), longer cycle times, higher purchase price. Brands: LG, Samsung, Electrolux, Bosch (compact), Miele (compact), Whirlpool, Maytag, GE.

**Compact (24").** European-style, 24" wide, stackable or side-by-side. 2.2–2.5 cu ft washer capacity. For condos, apartments, closet installations, secondary laundry. The Bosch 800 Series and Miele W1/T1 dominate this segment. Beko is the value alternative.

sections.title: Dryer Technology: Know the Difference
content: **Vented Electric.** Most common. Hot air passes through clothes, moisture-laden air is vented outside through a duct. Requires a 4" exterior vent. If the customer has an existing dryer hookup, it's almost certainly vented electric. 240V outlet required.

**Vented Gas.** Same principle, heated by a gas burner instead of an electric element. Slightly lower operating cost over time but higher purchase price. Requires gas line AND a vent. Less common in new construction but still popular in areas with low gas prices.

**Ventless Condensation.** No vent required — moisture condenses inside the dryer and drains to a tray or plumbing connection. Essential for installations without exterior wall access (interior closets, high-rises, basements). Longer dry times than vented. Bosch, Miele, Beko, LG, Samsung offer ventless.

**Heat Pump Dryer.** The most energy-efficient dryer technology available. Uses a refrigerant cycle to heat air (like an air conditioner in reverse). Uses roughly 50% less energy than conventional dryers. Ventless — no duct needed. Lower heat means gentler on fabrics. Trade-off: longer cycle times. Premium price. Bosch, Miele, Beko, LG, Whirlpool, Samsung. This is the technology that sells itself once you explain the energy savings — especially to condo buyers who can't vent.

**Washer-Dryer Combo.** One machine that washes and dries. Ventless. GE Profile UltraFast is the current leader — it actually works. Previous generations were terrible. The pitch: one machine, one load, walk away. Space savings are enormous. The trade-off: can't wash and dry simultaneously, and capacity is limited by the smaller of the two functions.

sections.title: Key Features and Selling Points
content: **Steam.** Available in washers and dryers. In washers: steam helps loosen stains and sanitize. In dryers: steam reduces wrinkles and refreshes clothes between washes. Good selling point for customers with allergies (sanitize cycle) or business attire (wrinkle reduction).

**WiFi/Smart.** Remote start, cycle notifications, diagnostic alerts. LG ThinQ, Samsung SmartThings, Whirlpool app, GE SmartHQ. The real value is the notification — knowing when the cycle is done so clothes don't sit in the washer and develop odor.

**Allergen/Sanitize Cycles.** Raises water temperature high enough to kill dust mites, pet dander, and bacteria. Important for families with allergies or asthma. Requires the washer to have an internal water heater — not all do.

**Auto-Dispense.** Bulk detergent reservoirs that automatically dose the right amount per load. LG, Samsung, Miele TwinDos. Eliminates the #1 laundry mistake: using too much detergent (which causes residue, odor, and machine damage).

**Pedestals.** Raise front-load washers and dryers to a comfortable loading height. Add storage drawers underneath. $250–$400 each. Almost every front-load buyer should be shown pedestals — they solve the bending complaint and add visible value.

sections.title: Capacity and Installation
content: **Standard capacity.** Full-size (27" wide): 4.5–5.8 cu ft washer, 7.0–9.0 cu ft dryer. Compact (24" wide): 2.2–2.5 cu ft washer, 4.0 cu ft dryer. The capacity numbers are drum volume — actual usable capacity is less.

**Stacking.** Front-load washers and compact units can be stacked (washer on bottom, dryer on top) with a stacking kit. Most stacking kits are $30–$80. Critical for closet installations, small laundry rooms, and condos. Not all brands' stacking kits are cross-compatible — verify.

**Electrical.** Full-size electric dryers need 240V/30A. Gas dryers need 120V + gas line. Washers need 120V standard outlet. Compact units typically run on 120V or 208/240V depending on the model — always check.

**Water connections.** Hot and cold supply lines, drain connection or standpipe. Flood protection features (hoses with auto-shutoff, leak sensors) are a legitimate add-on sale that protects the customer's home. Braided stainless steel hoses should replace rubber hoses on every installation.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
content: Open every washer door and dryer door on your floor. Load a blanket into a top-load agitator and then into a front-load — show the customer how much more room the front-load has. Know which units stack and which don't. Always ask where the laundry is being installed — the answer determines ventless vs vented, compact vs full-size, and stackable vs side-by-side.
